children: Over 25 years in public life, Narendra Modi’s policies have increasingly pushed India’s automobile industry towards manufacturing, localisation, electrification and exports, changing not just the size of the market, but its ambitions

Narendra Modi’s association with India’s automobile industry goes back much further than his years as Prime Minister of India. On October 7, 2001, Modi took oath as Gujarat Chief Minister, and he will complete his 25 years in public life on 7th October 2026. Today, as he turns 76, the automotive industry offers an interesting lens through which to examine those 25 years.
The bigger story is about how policy has attempted to change India's position in the global automotive value chain.
For decades, India was primarily seen as a large and attractive automobile market. Global manufacturers came here because Indians bought cars, motorcycles and commercial vehicles in large numbers.
The ambition during the Modi years has increasingly been different: make those vehicles, their components and their technologies in India and increasingly make them for markets outside India.
The Gujarat Chapter

The first chapter of this story was written in Gujarat. During Modi's tenure as Chief Minister, the state aggressively positioned itself as a manufacturing destination. The automobile industry became an important part of that strategy.

The 2008 shift of Tata Motors' Nano project from Singur to Sanand became one of the most visible examples. What followed was the development of a wider automotive ecosystem, with manufacturers, suppliers and ancillary companies setting up operations in the state.

The significance of this period goes beyond one car or one factory. It demonstrated an approach that would later become part of the national economic narrative, make it easier for manufacturers to invest, create industrial clusters, build infrastructure around them and attract the suppliers that make those clusters work.
When Modi moved to New Delhi in 2014, that thinking moved with him. Make in India was bigger than a factory programme The automobile industry was a natural fit for Make in India.

India already had a large domestic market, a substantial engineering workforce and a well-developed component industry. The challenge was to increase the depth of manufacturing and make India more relevant to global supply chains.

The scale of the industry today is considerably larger than it was three decades ago. Government data says vehicle production increased from about 2 million units in 1991-92 to around 28 million in 2023-24. The industry supports roughly 30 million direct and indirect jobs, according to the government. But the more revealing change is in the export ambition.

India is no longer simply producing vehicles to meet domestic demand. Passenger-vehicle exports have been growing, while India remains one of the world's largest producers of two-wheelers and three-wheelers.
The policy question has therefore moved from 'How many vehicles can India sell?' to “How much of the vehicle can India build, and where can that vehicle be sold?”
From Subsidies To Manufacturing

Electric vehicles provide perhaps the clearest example of how government policy has evolved. FAME and FAME II were primarily designed to encourage electric mobility through demand incentives and support for charging infrastructure. FAME II, which ran from 2019 to 2024, had total budgetary support of Rs 11,500 crore and supported approximately 16.72 lakh electric vehicles, according to the government.
But the policy conversation gradually moved beyond simply encouraging people to buy EVs.

The Rs 25,938-crore Production Linked Incentive scheme for automobiles and components, approved in 2021, was designed around Advanced Automotive Technology products. It includes electric vehicles and components and requires eligible applicants to achieve at least 50 per cent domestic value addition for incentives.
That is a significant shift. The government was no longer simply saying buy an EV. It was effectively saying build the technology here.

The numbers suggest that manufacturers have responded with significant investment. As of March 31, 2026, approved applicants under PLI Auto had reported investments of Rs 44,326 crore against a target of Rs 42,500 crore up to March 2027, according to the Ministry of Heavy Industries.
The EV Push Is Now An Ecosystem Story

PM E-DRIVE has taken the approach further. The scheme, with an outlay of Rs 10,900 crore, supports electric two- and three-wheelers, buses, trucks and ambulances, while also providing money for charging infrastructure and vehicle-testing facilities.

The government has allocated Rs 2,000 crore for public EV charging stations. As of July 2026, Rs 689 crore had been approved for 6,562 chargers through three oil marketing companies and nine states. The scheme had also supported more than 23 lakh EVs through reimbursed incentives by July 22, 2026.

The government itself has said that it has not yet conducted an assessment of the scheme's impact on accelerating EV adoption, reducing fossil-fuel consumption or lowering vehicle emissions. At the same time, it reported that EV penetration had risen from 0.7 per cent in FY2019-20 to 8.2 per cent in FY2025-26, alongside FAME II, PM E-DRIVE and other policies.
That distinction matters. The rise in EV adoption is measurable. Attributing all of that increase to one particular government scheme is a different claim.
The Less Visible Transformation

The most consequential part of this story may not be visible in a showroom. It is happening in batteries, electronics, motors, software, testing and components. The government's Rs 18,100-crore PLI scheme for Advanced Chemistry Cell battery manufacturing aims to establish a 50 GWh domestic manufacturing ecosystem. There is also increasing policy attention on critical components and rare-earth permanent magnets.
This is important because the future automobile is less mechanical than the one India became famous for manufacturing.

An EV requires batteries, power electronics, electric motors and sophisticated software. Even modern internal-combustion vehicles increasingly depend on electronics, sensors and connected technologies.
So localisation can no longer mean simply stamping body panels and assembling engines. The real test is how much technology India can develop and manufacture.
Infrastructure Completes The Picture

The automobile industry cannot be transformed through factories alone. Roads, freight infrastructure, logistics, charging networks and testing facilities determine how efficiently that manufacturing ecosystem works.

PM E-DRIVE's allocation for charging infrastructure and its Rs 780-crore provision for upgrading vehicle-testing agencies are examples of the government trying to address parts of that wider ecosystem.
There is also the vehicle-scrappage framework, which attempts to address the other end of the automobile lifecycle.

Taken together, these policies suggest that the government's automotive approach is broader than an EV policy. It covers manufacturing, taxation, technology, infrastructure, recycling, localisation and consumer demand.

This is where the Brand Modi automotive story becomes more complicated. Policy can encourage investment. It can reduce the cost of manufacturing. It can provide incentives for new technologies and build infrastructure. But it cannot guarantee that a technology will succeed in the market.

India still has to deal with the cost of batteries, charging availability, dependence on imported critical minerals, semiconductor and electronics supply chains, affordability of EVs and the transition for companies whose businesses are built around conventional powertrains.
There is also a much larger question. Can India move from being a manufacturing location to becoming a technology centre?

That will determine the next chapter. The government's policies have clearly increased the pressure on automakers and suppliers to localise and invest. But the real measure of success will ultimately be visible in the products themselves, what is engineered in India, what is patented here, what is manufactured here and what is exported from here.
The Road Ahead

There is no single Modi automotive policy. Instead, there is a collection of policies that have emerged over different stages: Make in India, FAME, PLI Auto, battery manufacturing incentives, PM E-DRIVE, charging infrastructure, vehicle scrappage and measures aimed at strengthening domestic supply chains.
India should not remain only one of the world's biggest automobile markets. It should become one of the world's important automobile manufacturing and technology bases.
Twenty-five years after Modi first became the head of a government, the Indian automobile industry is considerably larger and more ambitious than it was at the beginning of his political journey.

But the more important story is still being written. The next decade will show whether India's policy push can translate into deeper localisation, stronger Indian automotive technology, globally competitive suppliers and substantially higher exports.

That is ultimately where the automotive legacy of the Modi years will be measured, not by the number of policies announced, but by how much of the global automobile is eventually designed, engineered and built in India.
